analysis.title: What Next For US Politics And Equities?
key_insights: Democrats control Congress for the next two years but cannot undo Trump's tax and spending legislation. Overriding a veto or removing a president needs 2/3 of the Senate and Democrats will have 56 seats. TS Lombard calls the Democratic Congress a modest constraint rather than controlling.
The size of the Democratic majority reduces the sway of its extremist wing, since red states and red districts delivered it with centrist candidates. Working with Trump also helps Democrats in 2028.
Congress has limited ability to change the course of the Iran war. The War Powers Act has been worked around by presidents, and in 2006 Bush vetoed an Iraq funding bill with a withdrawal timetable.
Lame-duck and early-2027 priorities are raising the debt limit and setting FY27 appropriations including defence. The debt ceiling is the first large issue to resolve.

Ukraine, tariffs and ICE will be priorities in the new Congress, with investigations but no impeachment. Bipartisan pressure is expected on export controls for advanced technology sales to China and on Russia sanctions.
AI regulation is expected to get bipartisan support. AI power plants were a big election issue, and TX, OH and GA, which support building plants, flipped their governorships to Democrats.
Possible Trump-progressive deals on credit card costs and drug prices.

Since 2002 the S&P 500 generally rallies after mid-terms but underperforms its pre-election direction going in. The winning party does not explain market direction. In 2018 the S&P fell 9% from election day to year-end on Fed tightening, and in 2002 it fell 3.9% despite Republican seat gains. In four of six mid-terms since 2002 the market kept its pre-election direction.
VIX averages 21.9 pre-election and 19.5 post-election with no consistent trend. VIX near 20 compares with a median of 16.92 since Sep 2002 and is described as a non-event.
Rising negative sector correlations in Q4 versus Q3 point to a sector correction, not a broader bear market. Without GOOG and NVDA the S&P rose 0.8% in October.

The S&P 500 at 20.9x forward P/E is a 4.78% earnings yield, a 15-year doubling. That compares with 5.7% average nominal GDP growth over 10 years (13-year doubling) and a 4.9% 10Y zero-coupon yield (14-year doubling). TS Lombard calls the market fairly valued, with returns driven more by policy and geopolitics than rerating.
September JOLTS showed the hiring rate rising in information, lifting the private-sector total. TS Lombard sees this as year one of a recovery, with profits leading hiring.
TS Lombard expects the economy to improve in 2027 with inflation moving higher as growth continues and the Fed lags.

tension_points.bull_case: The S&P generally rallies after mid-terms. The market is fairly valued against nominal GDP and the 10Y, VIX is unextraordinary, and falling sector correlations point to a sector correction rather than a bear market.
tension_points.bear_case: Equity returns now depend on Trump's policies and the Fed, not rerating. Inflation is expected to rise as the Fed lags, and Trump is largely unconstrained by Congress. In 2018 the S&P fell 9% after the mid-terms on Fed tightening.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Fed tightening or a policy shock that reverses the post-mid-term pattern, as in 2018, or a market direction change that follows the pre-election trend (four of six mid-terms since 2002 kept the same direction).

theme_stances.key_argument: After mid-terms the equity market typically strengthens heading into year-end, and the market is fairly valued rather than in a broader bear market.
theme_stances.evidence: the equity market generally rallies after the mid-terms

theme_stances.key_argument: Congress cannot constrain Trump, so equity returns will depend on policy and the Fed rather than rerating.
theme_stances.evidence: Rerating is not the equity market's major problem going forward, policies are.
